title: Clean shipping lines
prompt: Customer names and cities were typed by hand, with stray spaces and odd capitals. Write `solve(customers)` so it returns `customer_id` and a tidy shipping `line` like `Ines Okafor, Leeds`.
rules: Tidy the name and the city the same way: no spaces at either end, exactly one space between words, and each word with a capital first letter and the rest in lower case.
`line` is the tidy name, a comma and a space, then the tidy city. If one of them is missing, `line` is just the other one, with no comma. If both are missing, `line` is empty text.
Return `customer_id` and `line`, in that order, for every customer, duplicates included.
hints: `F.trim` removes the outer spaces and `F.regexp_replace(col, r"\s+", " ")` turns every run of spaces into one. `F.initcap` fixes the capitals.
Apply the same tidy-up to both columns, then join them.
`concat` gives a missing result if any part is missing; `concat_ws(", ", a, b)` skips missing parts. Check what each gives when both parts are missing.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(customers):
    # customer_id, line
    return customers
explanation: Tidy each column with nested functions, `F.initcap(F.regexp_replace(F.trim(c), r"\s+", " "))`, then join with `concat_ws(", ", name, city)`. `concat_ws` skips a missing part, so a customer with no city gets just the name with no dangling comma, and when both parts are missing it returns empty text, not a missing value. `concat` would make the whole line missing as soon as one part is. `initcap` alone doesn't touch spaces, and `trim` only clears the ends: the double space in `ines   okafor` needs `regexp_replace`. The order of trim, replace and initcap doesn't matter.
